questions.problem: The length $l$ of a knife blade is $14\,\text{cm}$ to the nearest $1\,\text{cm}.$ Determine the upper and lower bounds of this measurement.
questions.worked_solution:
Our measurement is given to the nearest $1\,\text{cm}.$ So, the greatest possible error of this measurement is

$$
\frac{1\,\text{cm}}{2}=0.5\,\text{cm}.
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the lower and upper bounds of this measurement as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{lower bound} & =14\,\text{cm}-0.5\,\text{cm} \\  & =13.5\,\text{cm} \\ \text{upper bound} & =14\,\text{cm}+0.5\,\text{cm} \\  & =14.5\,\text{cm}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the exact value of $l$ lies between the lower and upper bound, we conclude that

$$
13.5\,\text{cm}\le l<14.5\,\text{cm}.
$$

questions.problem: The dimensions of the cover of a chemistry book are $28\,\text{cm}\times 14\,\text{cm}$, where each dimension is measured to the nearest $1\,\text{cm}.$ Rounded to the nearest square centimeter, what is the smallest possible area of the book's cover?
questions.worked_solution:
Each dimension is given to the nearest $1\,\text{cm}.$ So, the greatest possible error of these measurements is

$$
\frac{1\,\text{cm}}{2}=0.5\,\text{cm}.
$$

We wish to find the *smallest* possible area of the book's cover. Therefore, we require the *lower bound* of each dimension.

The lower bounds for each dimension are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 28\,\text{cm}-0.5\,\text{cm}=27.5\,\text{cm} \\  & 14\,\text{cm}-0.5\,\text{cm}=13.5\,\text{cm}\end{aligned}
$$

So,  the smallest possible area of the book's cover is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =27.5\,\text{cm}\times 13.5\,\text{cm} \\  & =371.25\,{\text{cm}}^{2} \\  & ≈371\,{\text{cm}}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest square centimeter.

canonical_examples.problem: The height $h$ of a lamppost is $30\,\textrm{ft}$ to the nearest $1\,\textrm{ft}.$ Determine the upper and lower bounds of this measurement.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Our measurement is given to the nearest $1\,\textrm{ft}.$ So, the greatest possible error of this measurement is

$$
\dfrac{1\,\textrm{ft}}{2} = 0.5\,\textrm{ft}.
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the lower and upper bounds of this measurement as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{lower bound} & =30\,\text{ft}-0.5\,\text{ft} \\  & =29.5\,\text{ft} \\ \text{upper bound} & =30\,\text{ft}+0.5\,\text{ft} \\  & =30.5\,\text{ft}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the exact value of $h$ lies between the lower and upper bound, we conclude that

$$
29.5\,\textrm{ft} \leq h <    30.5\,\textrm{ft}.
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding Bounds When Rounding to a Decimal Place
canonical_examples.problem: The area $a$ of a golf course measures $0.6\,\textrm{km}^2$ to the nearest tenth of a square kilometer. Determine the upper and lower bounds of this measurement.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Our measurement is given to the nearest $0.1\,\textrm{km}^2.$ So, the greatest possible error of this measurement is

$$
\dfrac{0.1\,\textrm{km}^2}{2} = 0.05\,\textrm{km}^2.
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the lower and upper bounds of this measurement as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{lower bound} & =0.6\,{\text{km}}^{2}-0.05\,{\text{km}}^{2} \\  & =0.55\,{\text{km}}^{2} \\ \text{upper bound} & =0.6\,{\text{km}}^{2}+0.05\,{\text{km}}^{2} \\  & =0.65\,{\text{km}}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the exact value of $a$ lies between the lower and upper bound, we conclude that

$$
0.55\,\textrm{km}^2 \leq a <            0.65\,\textrm{km}^2.
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Bounding Areas and Volumes
canonical_examples.problem: The dimensions of a parking lot are $90\, \textrm{m} \times 50\, \textrm{m}$, where each dimension is measured to the nearest $10\, \textrm{m}.$ Rounded to the nearest ten square meters, what is the upper bound for the area of the parking lot?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Each dimension is given to the nearest $10\,\textrm{m}.$ So, the greatest possible error of these measurements is

$$
\dfrac{10\,\textrm{m}}{2} = 5\,\textrm{m}.
$$

We wish to find the *upper bound* for the area of the parking lot. Therefore, we require the *upper bound* of each dimension.

The upper bounds for each dimension are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 90\,\text{m}+5\,\text{m}=95\,\text{m} \\  & 50\,\text{m}+5\,\text{m}=55\,\text{m}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the upper bound for the area of the parking lot is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =95\,\text{m}\times 55\,\text{m} \\  & =5\,225 \\  & ≈5\,230\,{\text{m}}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest ten square meters.

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
We always introduce **errors** in our measurements whenever we round or approximate numbers. In this lesson, we will explore how to quantify and describe measurement errors.

Suppose that a particular rope measures precisely $48.9\,\textrm{cm}.$ Now, imagine we take a meterstick and record a measurement of $50\,\textrm{cm}$ *to the nearest $10$ centimeters*. Let's mark this approximation on our meterstick.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14154806/assets/4e5d5ca05f27aa612b3fdcc9430b495870ddf540630857b6227897d6b20c9e89.png)

The error of a measurement equals the difference between the rounded estimate and the "true" value. So, in this example, the error of our approximation equals

$$
50\,\textrm{cm} - 48.9\,\textrm{cm} = 1.1\textrm{cm}.
$$

  

We often don't know the "true" measurement in practical problems. So, the next best thing is to determine a **lower bound** and an **upper bound** for our measurement:

- The *lower* bound of a measurement is its *smallest* possible value.

- The *upper* bound of a measurement is its *largest* possible value.

Let's figure out the lower and upper bounds of our $50\,\textrm{cm}$ approximation:

- The *lower bound* is $45 \, \textrm{cm}$ because this is the *smallest* value that gives $50 \, \textrm{cm}$ when rounded to the nearest $10\,\textrm{cm}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14154806/assets/da9cd6208cef81c6fe34fbba9b4271fa3ce1f30df69eb3c631ce6fea4f12e3a3.png)

- The *upper bound* is $55 \, \textrm{cm}$ because this is (almost) the *largest* value that gives $50 \, \textrm{cm}$ when rounded to the nearest $10\,\textrm{cm}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14154806/assets/23a195d88326b587e1864ef04e7b05f74d675f1ddc987baa2cf586af599eb4a9.png)

Let's use the letter $l$ to denote the "true" length of the rope. Then, we can combine our lower and upper bound measurements into a single statement, as follows:

$$
45\,\textrm{cm} \leq l \lt 55\,\textrm{cm}
$$

Notice that we used a *strict* "<" inequality for the upper bound. We cannot include $55\textrm{cm}$ in our set of values because this number rounds to $60\,\textrm{cm},$ not $50\,\textrm{cm}$.

We can visualize the lower and upper bounds on our diagram as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14154806/assets/1fdacb0787e8316a78da1ad65aa177e9a6f29215fa0d53aef88b0eb33326218d.png)

tutorials.name: The Greatest Possible Error
tutorials.problem:
So, we've seen how to calculate lower and upper bounds. Before we consider another example, note the following:

- The lower and upper bound depend on our approximation's **degree of accuracy**.

- In the last example, the degree of accuracy was $10\,\textrm{cm}$ because the rope was measured to the nearest $10$ centimeters.

- If we change the degree of accuracy, the lower and upper bounds will also change. So, for example, if we measured the rope to the nearest $1\,\textrm{cm},$ the lower and upper bounds would be different.

- The **greatest possible error** is the largest amount the "true" value can be from the approximation.

- This greatest possible error is always one-half of the degree of accuracy. So, in the last example, the greatest possible error in our measurement was

$$
\dfrac{10\,\textrm{cm}}{2} = {\color{blue}{5\,\textrm{cm}}}.
$$

We can use the greatest possible error to compute the lower and upper bounds quickly:

- To compute the lower bound of an approximation, we *subtract* the greatest possible error from the approximation. So, for the previous example, we have

$$
\textrm{lower bound} = 50\,\textrm{cm} - {\color{blue}{5\,\textrm{cm}}} = 45\,\textrm{cm.}
$$

- To compute the upper bound of an approximation, we *add* the greatest possible error to the approximation. So, for the previous example, we have

$$
\textrm{upper bound} = 50\,\textrm{cm} + {\color{blue}{5\,\textrm{cm}}} = 55\,\textrm{cm.}
$$

Let's see another example.
